title: The Peacemaker Unites the Five Nations
text:
Haudenosaunee tradition tells of a time when the nations south of Lake Ontario were locked in endless revenge killings. Into this world came a man known as the Peacemaker, who carried a message of peace, power and righteousness.

His first great ally was Hiawatha, a man so stricken with grief after his daughters died that he wandered alone in the forest. The Peacemaker found him, and with strings of shell beads spoke words to wipe away his tears and clear his mind. That ritual, in the tradition, became the condolence ceremony still used to raise up new chiefs.

Together they went from nation to nation. The Mohawk, Oneida, Cayuga and Seneca agreed to the peace. The hardest to win was Tadodaho of the Onondaga, a fearsome leader said to have snakes twisting in his hair. In the end they combed the snakes out and made him the keeper of the council fire, with the Onondaga hosting the great council.

The Peacemaker planted a white pine as the Tree of Peace. The leaders threw their weapons into a hole beneath its roots, and an eagle was set on top to watch for danger. In one version he showed them that a single arrow snaps easily, while five bound together cannot be broken. The Five Nations became a confederacy governed by the Great Law of Peace, and in the early eighteenth century the Tuscarora joined as a sixth nation.
lesson: Former enemies can unite when grief is acknowledged and the strongest holdout is given an honored role. A bundle of arrows is stronger than any single one.
location: Haudenosaunee homelands, New York State, USA
source: Haudenosaunee oral tradition of the Great Law of Peace (Kaianere'ko:wa); Arthur C. Parker, The Constitution of the Five Nations (1916)
caveat: This is a traditional account; scholars date the founding of the confederacy anywhere from the twelfth to the sixteenth century.
